PartitionGuard copies the bounds-checking logic of Partition (`start_block`, `check_access`, and `within_bounds` in lib.rs) instead of sharing it, so a later fix to one copy can silently miss the other. In esa.rs, the guard's read/write/erase bodies (lines ~265-312) repeat the Partition bodies except that they call `self.guard` instead of `self.storage.lock().await`.

Holding a PartitionGuard blocks every other partition on the same device, because they all share one mutex. If a task awaits any Partition operation (or `lock()` on another partition) while holding a guard, it waits forever, and neither the docs nor the README warn about this. `lock()` returns a guard that holds `self.storage.lock().await`. Every partition shares that `&Mutex<M, F>` (test/mod.rs map). The test at test/bdd.rs:128-132 confirms that holding `factory.lock()` makes `settings.try_lock()` fail. The doc comment only says 'The underlying mutex is held for the lifetime of this guard'. README.md:76 describes the Mutex but not the new lock API.

`lock()` and `try_lock()` lock the mutex for the whole device, which every partition from the same `PartitionManager` shares. A `PartitionGuard` therefore blocks every other partition on the device, not just this one; the tests confirm this, since holding `factory.lock()` makes `settings.try_lock()` fail. The docs say the guard gives exclusive access to "a partition's underlying storage" and don't warn about this. If a task holds a guard and then calls a normal `Partition` method (on this or any other partition of the device) in the same task, it deadlocks forever. The PR's motivation is panic handlers, but `try_lock()` doesn't really deliver that. Every operation on the returned guard (`read`/`write`/`erase`) is `async`, and a `#[panic_handler]` or other sync context can't await without its own executor or block_on. Also, in typical no_std builds (panic=abort / panic-probe), a panicking task never releases the lock, so try_lock will always fail there. The documentation should say what the supported use case is, or a blocking API should be provided, so users don't build crash-logging on an assumption that doesn't hold. Lines 390-394: on EEXIST with `--push`, the marker is 'not re-written', Step 4b is skipped and the flow goes 'directly to Step 4c'. Step 4c then reads `.clancy/plans/{stem}.md` (line 504) and posts its content through the curl blocks. Nothing in 4a's retry branch or in 4c hashes the plan and compares it to the marker's `sha256=`, even though lines 410-412 describe that comparison as the gate. Trigger: approve plan X, the push fails, edit X.md, then run the printed retry command `/clancy:approve-plan X --push --ticket KEY`. The edited content is posted to the ticket while the marker still holds the old hash. The same branch also re-posts a duplicate comment when the earlier push succeeded, because it never checks for a prior `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN_PUSH` row.

The bracketed-key Source parser cannot match Notion keys (hex/UUID) or Shortcut-style keys, so Notion auto-detect never pushes and Notion Sources are wrongly classed as 'file-path'. The pushable pattern is `^\[(#?\d+|[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*-\d+)\]\s+.+$`, which allows only `#digits`, bare digits or `UPPER-digits`. Brief writes board Sources as `[{KEY}] {Title}` (brief.md:808), and Notion keys are `^[0-9a-f]{32}$|^[0-9a-f-]{36}$` (line 186 table). So `[3f2a…] Title` falls into bucket 3 ('matches anything else', line 526). That logs `BOARD_PUSH_SKIPPED_NO_TICKET | file-path` and shows 'source is file-path', which is wrong. The Notion success note added to Step 7 (line 1504) can then only fire through `--ticket`. Shortcut's `[SC-123]`, which Step 2 line 106 accepts, parses as bracketed but then hard-errors against `^\d+$`.

The trigger is a corrupt or partly written file at verify time, so this is an unusual path. A fix is to wrap the parse in try/catch, print a fixed message and call `process.exit(1)`.
